content: The Consolidated Guideline on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights of Women Living with HIV was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2017. This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations and good practice statements to address the sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) of women living with HIV. It emphasizes the importance of gender equality and human rights in improving the quality of life and health outcomes for these women. The guideline highlights that HIV not only exacerbates gender inequality but also leaves women more vulnerable to its effects. In 2015, approximately 8 million women aged 15 and older were living with HIV, representing 51% of all adults with the condition. Adolescent girls and young women are disproportionately affected, accounting for 60% of young people aged 15–24 living with HIV and 58% of new infections in this age group. Many women living with HIV face inequitable access to quality health services and experience intersecting forms of stigma, discrimination, and violence, including violations of their sexual and reproductive rights. Since the publication of WHO’s 2006 guidelines on the care and treatment of women living with HIV, significant advancements have been made in HIV-related policies, research, and practices. This new guideline consolidates existing recommendations with updated evidence and good practice statements to better support healthcare providers, program managers, and policymakers in addressing the SRHR of women living with HIV. The guideline adopts a woman-centered approach, which prioritizes the perspectives, needs, and rights of women, their families, and communities. It emphasizes the importance of respecting women’s autonomy in health-related decision-making and providing them with the information and options needed to make informed choices. This approach is grounded in two guiding principles: the promotion of human rights and gender equality. Human rights are central to ensuring the dignity and well-being of women living with HIV. This includes the right to the highest attainable standard of health, freedom from violence, equality, and non-discrimination. The right to sexual and reproductive health is an integral part of the right to health, as outlined in international human rights frameworks. Gender equality is also critical, as unequal power dynamics, harmful gender norms, and limited access to resources significantly impact women’s access to and experiences with health services. The guideline development process involved a global survey to capture the SRHR priorities of women living with HIV, ensuring their voices were central to the recommendations. The guideline also addresses the need to create an enabling environment to overcome barriers to service uptake and engagement. These barriers, which exist at individual, interpersonal, community, and societal levels, include stigma, social exclusion, gender-based violence, and criminalization. Strategies are needed across health system components to improve the accessibility, acceptability, affordability, and quality of services for women living with HIV. Implementation of the guideline requires evidence-informed strategies tailored to local contexts and responsive to the needs and rights of women living with HIV. Effective implementation may involve reorganizing care and redistributing healthcare resources, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The guideline will be updated every five years or sooner if significant new evidence emerges. It aims to support countries in planning, developing, and monitoring programs that promote gender equality and human rights, ultimately improving health outcomes for women living with HIV.
